## Intent
Hypothesis: Halide parallelization of the expressible math loop (LP1) can approach the streaming ceiling even when the RNG-order loop (LP2) is not Halide-expressible.

## Cache saturation
All tested N (10000–10000000) exceed the L2 spill at N≈7710. N=10000 and N=100000 are L3-resident (680 KB and 6.8 MB vs 16 MB L3); N=1000000 and N=10000000 spill to DRAM (68 MB and 680 MB). Yet ns/p stays FLAT across this range: at death_q=0.01, 41.6–42.9 ns/p with no L3→DRAM knee. Death rate raises the floor without reshaping the curve — q=0.5 holds at 52.6–54.5 ns/p — confirming per-particle overhead dominates, not cache capacity.

## Bandwidth
Peak is 1.63 GB/s at N=10000000, q=0.01 — 12.8% of the 12.69 GB/s ceiling. Bandwidth is flat across N (1.58–1.63 GB/s at q=0.01), so the algo is overhead-bound, not bandwidth-bound. Death rate scales it down proportionally (1.63→1.29 GB/s, q=0.01→0.5). The profile confirms: threads=1 shows 58.8% frontend stall, 41.2% compute, 0% backend; threads=4/8 degrade to ~90% frontend stall with compute collapsing to 4–8%.

## Assembly
No vectorization — 0 vector-suffixed instructions in 440 insns. All FP is scalar: `vmulss` (4), `vaddss` (1), `vsubss` (1), `vucomiss` (11), `vmovss` (15); `vmovaps` (9) and `vxorps` (3) are stack-init only. Loop1 calls `halide_b5_math`; loop2 processes particles individually with scalar loads (`vmovss xmm0,DWORD PTR [r14]`), scalar compares, and byte-granular scatter stores (`mov BYTE PTR [r13+r14*1+0x0],sil`). The 27 `cmp`, 12 `cmovae`, 11 `jae` create a branch-dense path explaining the 58.8% frontend stall; scalar code and byte stores cap bandwidth at 13% of ceiling.

## Verdict
Refuted — the algo reaches only 1.63 GB/s = 12.8% of the 12.69 GB/s ceiling with 0 vector instructions and 58.8% frontend stall (rising to ~90% at threads=4/8). The Halide-expressible math loop does not approach streaming performance because the compiler emits only scalar FP (`vmulss`, `vaddss`, `vsubss`) and the non-Halide RNG-order loop dominates with byte-granular scatter writes and branch-heavy per-particle logic, leaving the algo frontend-bound at every N and death rate.
